tags.gist: Says supervisory agents can help and the commenter uses one, but their reliability is the whole question and the failure mode is quite specific.
Reports four occasions in one session when a model acting as reviewer made confident assertions its evidence could not support, caught only by the operator.
Notes the agent disclosed its evidence's age only when challenged, used one register regardless of evidence quality, and left sound and unsound conclusions indistinguishable.
Says intent is not a useful axis, since calling the outputs errors or misstatements changes nothing for someone relying on them.
Details the four occasions: inverted causation, a sentence never spoken, a rule remembered rather than executed, and the present answered from a stale copy.
Finds one failure kind in all four: correct evidence was available but a cheaper proxy was reported as measurement, and proxy-record agreement is no corroboration.
Argues the failure is disclosure order: a caveat after challenge is a concession, and an agent reporting normal from unconfirmed data gives a false finding.
Recommends evaluating supervisory agents on four observable properties of unsupported, undisclosed assertions, avoiding any standard that turns on candour or intent.
Wants supervisory agents validated on cases the operator cannot independently check, without carrying expert-in-the-loop performance over to unsupervised use.
Would require an agent to emit the artifact consulted and its timestamp with each finding, before the finding rather than on request.
Would count a present-tense answer taken from a copy older than a set limit as a failure, not something to caveat.
Would bar an agent from vouching for a component it belongs to, and discount agreement with a device log when both share an instrument.
Would validate agents against output that cannot be checked against a reference at the point of use, rather than against a benchmark set.
Would require every assertion to be labeled with its evidence class, measured, cached or inferred, so reviewers can filter rather than infer from tone.
Wants monitoring programs to say what happens when no one in the loop can catch an error, and not to treat operator acceptance as validation.
Clarifies this is a single uncontrolled session with a commercial assistant, offered as a failure class rather than an error rate.
Does not seek to exclude supervisory agents, noting the same agent helped and misled within one hour with no way to tell which.
Takes no position on whether the behavior is error or something stronger, holding that the standard should leave that question out.
Says the commenter's users cannot check, so a supervisory agent wrongly reporting their device fine is a monitoring failure that looks like normal operation.
